analysis.one_liner: Funds transit, rail, bike, and sidewalk projects with proceeds from auctioning greenhouse gas emission allowances.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2009 by Senator Carper with a Republican co-sponsor but never got a committee vote or floor action before that Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Low Greenhouse Gas Transportation Fund by auctioning 10% of emission allowances each year from 2012 through 2050 under any EPA cap-and-trade program in effect. It would require states and large metro areas to write 10-year plans to cut transportation emissions, and spend at least 80% of the fund on projects like new transit service, intercity passenger rail, bike paths, sidewalks, freight rail, and carpool programs, with an 80% federal cost share. Plans could not use the money to add lanes for single-occupant cars, and funding would be weighted toward mobility for low-income people, minorities, the elderly, and households without a car. Everything hinged on a national cap-and-trade law, which never passed.
analysis.who_benefits: Transit riders, pedestrians, and cyclists in states and metropolitan areas that write qualifying emission-reduction plans; the bill explicitly directs funding toward low-income individuals, minorities, the elderly, the disabled, households without a car, and cost-burdened households paying more than 30% of income for housing. State and local governments benefit from an 80% federal cost share for the projects.

how_it_helps.text: Requires states and metro areas representing more than 200,000 people to set 10-year goals to reduce transportation greenhouse gas emissions and write integrated reduction plans, and funds transit, intercity rail, bicycle and pedestrian projects, freight rail, carpooling, and telecommuting programs under those plans [S2].

Targets funding to increase mobility options for low-income individuals, minorities, the elderly, disabled people, households without cars, and cost-burdened households, and requires plans to analyze impacts on access to jobs, health care, and education for elderly and economically disadvantaged communities [S3].
Bars the fund's money from being used for new general-purpose highway lanes or added capacity for single-occupant vehicles, and provides an 80% federal share for funded projects [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The businesses that would have to buy emission allowances at auction under the EPA cap-and-trade program generating the fund's revenue — mainly fossil fuel users and emitters — whose costs could be passed on to consumers through higher energy prices. Highway-focused projects would also lose access to this new funding stream.

drawbacks.text: The entire funding mechanism depends on an EPA cap-and-trade program that never existed; with no auction revenue, the fund would hold nothing and the transit projects would go unfunded [S2].
Auction costs would fall on regulated emitters, and those costs could be passed to households through higher energy prices [S2].
States and metro areas would face a federal mandate to produce and update greenhouse gas reduction plans and could have funding withheld for noncompliance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-side benefits were real but conditional: more transit, safer walking and biking, and an explicit equity focus, paid for by pricing emissions rather than by general taxes. The bill's fatal weakness was structural — it created a fund fed by a cap-and-trade program that Congress never enacted, so the whole scheme was a rider on separate legislation that also died. Had the climate bill passed, the costs to energy users would have been significant and would partly have flowed through to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in March 2009 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, it sat there with no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action until that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Thomas Carper, joined by Senator Arlen Specter, introduced the bill in the Senate on March 11, 2009 [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which was its only committee action [S5].
It attracted seven cosponsors — six Democrats and one Republican [S4].
The bill's funding mechanism was contingent on a separate EPA cap-and-trade program auctioning emission allowances; no such program was enacted during the 111th Congress [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no new allowance-auction revenue stream was created and no new federal requirements fell on states and metropolitan planning organizations; emitters and energy users never faced the allowance charge, and existing highway and transit funding patterns continued unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Thomas R. Carper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Senator Carper.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 11, 2009 and took no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no report — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with a Republican co-introducer and seven cosponsors split 6-1 — but no vote was ever held to test broader support.

industries.industry: Public transit, intercity passenger rail, and bicycle/pedestrian infrastructure
industries.note: The bill would route at least 80% of a new federal fund into transit expansion, passenger rail, sidewalks, and bike facilities — projects riders would use directly. Transit operators and construction firms would gain as delivery channels, but the public benefit is the point of the spending.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel and other greenhouse gas emitters subject to cap-and-trade
industries.note: These businesses would have to buy the auctioned allowances that fill the fund, a cost that could be passed to consumers through higher energy prices. The fund's purpose — reducing petroleum-based vehicle travel — runs against their sales.
The bill aims to reduce miles driven and petroleum-derived fuel use, shrinking demand over time. Higher transit and telecommuting options substitute for their product.

industries.industry: Highway construction and single-occupant road expansion
industries.note: Plans funded under the bill may not include new general-purpose vehicle lanes, so this new money stream excludes traditional road-widening work. Existing federal highway programs would be untouched.
